title: Arrival in Idaho; family background
description: The interviewer begins collecting biographical data. The interviewee says she came to Idaho on May 25, 1949, settled at 970 Spruce Street in Potlatch, and discusses her mother Mildred, a housewife born in 1891 who died in 1955, and her father Herbert, whose family came from Germany.Potential biographical information on her family origins is discussed.

title: Father's work; siblings; marriage and children
description: She talks about her father's farm and railroad work on the Milwaukee Road, and lists her siblings including her twin brothers Herbert and Maynard. She then describes marrying Raymond in Iron Mountain, Michigan, in 1934 and names her children with their birth dates and jobs.

title: Jobs; Royal Neighbors club
description: The interviewee recalls the jobs she held over the years: waitress, clerk, short-order cook, and potato harvesting, where she once made over a hundred dollars in six weeks. She also mentions belonging to the Royal Neighbors lodge that met above the big store.

title: Childhood work; class differences; parenting views
description: She describes her childhood picking wild berries in Wisconsin and walking ten miles to sell them, and contrasts the self-entertaining life of children then with television-era kids. She reflects on class prejudice against the poor, how people treat each other more equally now, and her belief that parents should let children choose their own paths.

title: Early Potlatch company town
description: The interviewee describes Potlatch when she arrived, with wooden sidewalks and houses owned and maintained by the Potlatch lumber company, which sent crews to paint and clean. She worked taking inventory at a privately owned business and notes the whole town was company property.

title: Local entertainment; Riverside hall; floods
description: She recalls the town's movie theater, which showed a different film every Saturday, and the Riverside building by the bridge that housed a dance hall and roller-skating rink where big-name bands like Ernest Tubb played. She also remembers floods that damaged the building and the dam that broke.

title: Childbirth; Rh factor losses
description: The interviewee recounts having children at home and in hospital, and losing her son Jerry and a stillborn baby girl to Rh blood factor complications that were not understood at the time. She describes the difficult labor, the long drive to the doctor, and the treatments such as blood transfusions and exchange transfusions that were just emerging after World War Two.

title: Blood transfusions; RH factor
description: The interviewee discusses wartime blood transfusions, recalling that whole blood could be fatal and that many patients died before the RH factor was discovered. She explains in simple terms how the presence or absence of the factor distinguishes blood types.

title: War years at home; draft deferments
description: The interviewee says she could not volunteer because her children were small, noting Jim was born in October 1941 just before Pearl Harbor. She explains that Jerome was always deferred from the draft because his work was crucial, though younger local men left for service.

title: Local Japanese families; internment
description: The interviewee recalls that houses in a nearby field once belonged to Japanese families who were removed to internment camps before her family arrived. She is unsure of details but believes they were taken from the area and put in camps.

title: Brothers' Pacific service; kamikaze attacks; war trauma
description: She tells how her brothers Red and Herb served in World War II, with Red on a destroyer near Pearl Harbor enduring kamikaze attacks and rescuing men from blood-slicked decks. Red later suffered laughing and crying spells, and she reflects on how much horror a person can bear.

title: Brother's Army service; Holocaust photographs
description: She recounts her other brother's Army service in Europe, where he photographed concentration camp victims, mass graves dug by bulldozers, and starved Polish forced laborers. He only showed the graphic pictures to family several years after the war.

title: Korean War; Pacific island fighting; Japanese refusal to surrender
description: She mentions Jack's destroyer service in 1952 during the Korean War, then returns to Red's accounts of island assaults where Japanese soldiers would not surrender. She describes clearing caves with grenades, a woman with a baby who attacked with a hidden grenade, and the H-bomb as the only thing that forced Japan's surrender.

title: End of the war; nuclear fears; oil politics; rebuilding Japan
description: The conversation shifts to the postwar period, with the interviewer expressing nuclear-age anxieties and the interviewee discussing the oil crisis, Kissinger's peace talks, and gas shortages she suspects are political gimmicks. She also complains that the United States rebuilt Japan's factories after destroying them in the war.

title: Rising prices; sugar and clothing costs
description: The interviewee complains about inflation, noting gas shortages that vanish at vacation time and sugar prices that jumped from five to fourteen dollars. She describes shopping for coats and blouses, citing sale prices of thirty-six to forty-eight dollars and the poor quality of modern fabrics.

title: Interview permissions and wrap-up
description: The pair discuss the interview project, including a request to withhold the interviewee's name from a presentation, release forms, and permission to use the material. The interviewer mentions doing this work rather than taking classes.
